title: “TEST ME IN THIS” — The Verse Prosperity Preachers Love… But Malachi Was Never a Get-Rich Formula
paragraphs:
“TEST ME IN THIS” — The Verse Prosperity Preachers Love… But Malachi Was Never a Get-Rich Formula
God really did say, “Test Me.” But before you turn Malachi 3:10 into a promise that giving money will make you rich, you need to hear what God was actually confronting—and why the truth is far more dangerous to your heart than a prosperity sermon.
There is something almost shocking about Malachi 3:10.

Especially when they are pulled out of their setting, placed beneath a giving envelope, projected onto a church screen, or followed by a testimony about somebody who gave their last hundred dollars and mysteriously received a thousand the next week.
You have probably heard some version of it.
“Give, and God will give you more.”
“Release what is in your hand so God can release what is in His.”
“God said to test Him. Try Him. Give your tithe and watch what happens to your finances.”
“Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse... Test me in this... and see if I will not throw open the floodgates of heaven and pour out so much blessing...”
Christianity becomes an investment strategy with heaven as the bank.
That is not what Malachi was saying.
And if we reduce this passage to a divine wealth formula, we may actually repeat the very spiritual sickness Malachi was confronting.
Because Malachi 3 is not primarily about people discovering the secret to becoming wealthy.
It is about a people who belonged to God while withholding from God.
And underneath the money was something much deeper.
“Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse.”
The storehouse—בֵּית הָאוֹצָר (bêṯ hāʾôṣār)—belongs to the world of Israel’s covenant worship and temple economy.
This was not Malachi introducing a twenty-first-century fundraising technique.
He was speaking to covenant Israel.
The Old Testament tithe existed within Israel’s covenant life, involving agricultural produce, livestock, support for the Levites, worship, communal celebration, and provision for vulnerable people.
Suddenly the passage begins breathing in its own world again.
God was not standing before modern Christians saying:
“Transfer ten percent to a ministry and I guarantee financial multiplication.”
He was confronting His covenant people because something had gone terribly wrong in their relationship with Him.
And Malachi had already exposed it.
Their giving problem was a worship problem.
Their worship problem was a heart problem.
And heart problems have a strange ability to hide behind religious appearances.
You can sing while withholding yourself.
You can pray while protecting an idol.
You can attend church while quietly telling Jesus:
“You may have this part of me, Lord.
Money merely has a remarkable ability to reveal where that boundary has been drawn.
That is why Jesus spoke about money so penetratingly.
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Jesus understood something we desperately want to avoid.
Our bank statements can sometimes expose our theology more honestly than our worship songs.
But that still does not make Malachi 3:10 a get-rich formula.
Now we reach the famous words:
The verb comes from בחן (bḥn), carrying the idea of examining, testing, or proving.
God really does invite Israel to test Him here.
We should not explain that away simply because the verse has been abused.
But we must allow God to define the test.
Not our desire for financial security.
Israel had withheld what belonged within its covenant obligations, and God called the nation to return to covenant faithfulness and discover that He Himself remained faithful.
That is dramatically different from saying:
“Give God money and He is contractually obligated to make you rich.”
Then comes the image everybody remembers:
God speaks about rebuking the “devourer,” protecting the fruit of the ground, preventing the vine from failing, and the nations recognizing Israel's blessed condition.
It echoes the covenant blessings and curses found in the Torah.
The passage is not describing God turning every faithful worshiper into a millionaire.
It is describing God's faithfulness toward covenant Israel in categories deeply connected with the covenant under which Israel lived.
And that distinction matters because Christians live under the new covenant established through Jesus Christ.
So does that mean Malachi 3 has nothing to say to Christians?
It means we must receive what it actually says before applying it through Christ.
And what it says may be more confronting than “give ten percent.”
Because ten percent can become comfortable.
Ten percent can become another box.
Ten percent can even become a way of saying:
The remaining ninety percent is mine.”
Then Jesus walks into the room.
And suddenly the conversation becomes much more serious.
Jesus does not merely claim ten percent.
“How little must I surrender while still qualifying as obedient?”
That destroys both greed and religious bargaining.
The New Testament does not present Christian generosity as a vending machine where you insert money and receive material prosperity.
“Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.”
“Give tonight or God will withhold your breakthrough.”
“Sow into this ministry and your debt will disappear.”
“Send your seed and expect a hundredfold financial return.”
Christian giving is rooted in grace.
And Paul gives us the supreme model in 2 Corinthians 8:9:
“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that you by His poverty might become rich.”
Before someone turns that into another prosperity slogan, look at the surrounding chapters.
Christ is not presented as a technique for acquiring luxury.
“Give Jesus something so He will make you rich.”
“You were spiritually bankrupt, and the Son of God gave Himself to rescue you.”
You had a debt you could never pay.
You had guilt you could never erase.
You had righteousness you could never manufacture.
You were separated from God by sin.
And the risen Christ became our hope.
That is wealth no market can measure.
So perhaps the most dangerous question Malachi 3:10 raises for us is not:
“If I give more money, how much will God give me back?”
“Do I actually trust God enough to loosen my grip?”
Because money promises many of the things only God can ultimately provide.
And suddenly our theology starts trembling.
Then someone else gets the house.
That is where Malachi still finds us.
Not because the church is ancient Israel.
Not because every Christian is promised agricultural covenant prosperity.
Not because tithing functions as a heavenly investment scheme.
But because the God who confronted divided worship then still sees divided worship now.
Maybe you have been using God financially.
Maybe giving became gambling dressed in Christian vocabulary.
Maybe somebody taught you that generosity guaranteed wealth, and when the wealth never arrived, you quietly wondered whether God had failed you.
Maybe you gave desperately because someone promised a miracle.
Maybe you emptied an account you could not afford to empty because a preacher implied that the size of your sacrifice determined the size of your breakthrough.
And now you are ashamed to admit that nothing happened the way you were promised.
Malachi 3:10 did not promise you that transaction.
God did not break a promise He never made.
Or perhaps your struggle is the opposite.
But giving still feels like losing.
You tip generously at restaurants but become irritated when someone talks about supporting Gospel work.
but when the Kingdom asks something from you, suddenly every dollar becomes sacred.
Not because every Christian must fund every ministry.
Not because saying no to a fundraising appeal is sinful.
And certainly not because anybody should manipulate you by claiming that refusing to give means refusing God.
Zacchaeus encountered Jesus, and money suddenly lost its throne.
The Macedonian believers experienced grace, and generosity overflowed even amid severe hardship.
The earliest Christians saw brothers and sisters in need and opened their possessions.
Because when Christ becomes your treasure, possessions stop being your master.
That is the part prosperity theology often misses.
The greatest blessing is not that Jesus helps you possess more.
It is that Jesus frees you from being possessed by what you possess.
Because someday money may tighten its grip around your heart again, and you may need to remember:
Jesus did not die so greed could become baptized ambition.
He died to make you His.
And this is where I must be careful even with what I am about to ask you.
Mission requires people willing to give, serve, share, pray, create, and sacrifice.
But after everything we have just said about Malachi 3, it would be hypocritical for me to manipulate you.
So I will not tell you:
“Give to Gospel Warrior and God owes you a financial breakthrough.”
Your salvation was purchased by Christ.

But if Gospel Warrior is genuinely helping you love Scripture, understand the Gospel, repent of sin, endure suffering, grow in Christ, and reach people who desperately need biblical truth, then supporting that work can become one practical expression of generosity.
And if you genuinely want to glorify God through helping sound Gospel-centered truth reach more people, do not assume support must always mean money.
Someone you went to school with.
Someone who believes God abandoned them because the financial miracle they were promised never happened.
Someone smiling in photographs while privately drowning.
Someone who would never walk into your church.
You can put this article in front of them.
Not to make an algorithm happy.
Has money ever become too important to you?
Have you ever been hurt by prosperity teaching?
Have you ever treated God like a transaction?
Or are you currently struggling to trust Him financially?
Sometimes repentance begins when hiding ends.
Not because every paragraph is easy.
Because some truths need to be reread when the emotional moment has passed.
But understand why I am inviting you.
Not because God will love you more.
Not because Malachi 3:10 guarantees that the money will return multiplied.
If you want to support that mission:
And remember something before you leave.
God does not need your money.
The question has always been whether your money owns you.
Malachi confronted a people withholding from God.
Jesus went deeper and called people to surrender themselves.
And at the cross, Christ did not merely give ten percent for you.
So when you hear the words—
do not hear the voice of a heavenly salesman promising luxury in exchange for a seed.
Hear the covenant God exposing unbelief.
Hear the Father calling His people away from divided worship.
Then look beyond Malachi toward Calvary and see the ultimate evidence that God can be trusted.
Not because every faithful Christian becomes wealthy.
Not because believers never experience poverty.
Not because generosity guarantees an easy life.
Trust Him because while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Trust Him because the cross proves His love more decisively than your bank balance ever could.
Trust Him when the harvest is abundant.
Trust Him when the field looks empty.
Trust Him when you can give freely.
Trust Him when you must receive humbly.
Trust Him when there is plenty.
Trust Him when your prayer sounds like:
“Give us this day our daily bread.”
And whatever God places in your hands...
Because eventually every house will belong to someone else.
Every investment account will be left behind.
Every expensive thing you once desperately wanted will become outdated, broken, forgotten, sold, or thrown away.
And maybe that is the blessing our prosperity-obsessed generation desperately needs to rediscover:
Not “Jesus as the path to wealth.”
Not even “Jesus instead of financial responsibility.”
Because the greatest proof that God is good was never a bigger paycheck.
You do not need Jesus to make everything you own more valuable; you need Jesus to show you that everything becomes small beside the value of knowing Him.
